title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent-to-configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators (a containerized Batfish instance and a Python graph-based static reachability analyzer), and a matched sample of N=300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented with gpt-5-mini under a preregistered protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The run completed the planned 600 episodes, consuming 300 model calls and recording zero failed episodes. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Importantly, verifier checks never reported forbidden reachability and the GVR repair step was never invoked; thus the experiment measures whether inserting a verifier changes observed compliance when baseline generation already meets the safety predicate, not whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We report artifact-backed execution and analysis results and discuss design choices (shared-initial-generation semantics, adversarial strength, repair budget) that explain the null and guide future stress-testing protocols.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) can speed operations but risks introducing security-relevant errors such as unauthorized reachability or policy violations. Prior systems and surveys therefore recommend integrating execution-capable validators or generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops to detect and correct hazardous outputs. We test a focused, preregistered confirmatory question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline under a deterministic paired evaluation? Contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specifying a paired N=300 design and prespecified analyses; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution using FRRouting-style images and two deterministic validators; and (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing that, for the selected task set and model (gpt-5-mini), baseline single-pass generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate on every tested intent, so a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline produced no measurable improvement.
sections.related_work: Three relevant strands motivate this study. (1) Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness on code and IaC benchmarks; these results motivate verifier-in-the-loop designs but show variable gains depending on task and verifier strength. Representative system papers include TerraFormer (automated IaC with verifier feedback) and other recent GVR demonstrations. (2) Surveys and NetOps studies document LLM risks (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight. (3) Work on emulation/testbed platforms demonstrates that execution-based validation is feasible in research settings but highlights external-validity gaps. Our experiment sits at the intersection: an execution-validated, preregistered paired test of verifier insertion for an operationally meaningful safety predicate (forbidden reachability). All cited records were verified during the autonomous literature pass and are listed in the bibliography.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered a paired design (study id cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). Sampling: fixed matched sample N=300 (150 benign seeds × 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Intervention: per intent pair execute (A) baseline: single-pass LLM generation (one LLM call) and (B) guarded: LLM initial generation + verifier check + up to one LLM repair attempt (GVR). The preregistered GVR repair policy invoked a repair only when a validator reported forbidden reachability; at most one repair call per pair was allowed. Execution contract: shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (the same initial LLM candidate was used for both baseline and guarded playback), producing one model call per pair (hence model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs). Validators and environment: experiments ran deterministically in Docker compositions using FRRouting-style router images and two deterministic validators: (i) a containerized Batfish instance and (ii) a Python graph-based static reachability analyzer. Per-episode scoring artifacts record validator provenance fields validator_id='deterministic_netops_validator_v5' and validator_version='5.0' (see representative scoring traces such as execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; SHA-256: bec01d9f0e25d35a4d503d271742ba466b52606aa4b035ed70e3a4ba66779bb7). Detailed validator artifacts (Batfish container image, policy files, and the Python analyzer implementation) and the full execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json; the raw model outputs file execution/raw_results.jsonl has SHA-256 36ea4a5dfa90384f2a388cba4f39bf193bb3c150ea22ca60957facb20ca960f1). Outcome and analysis: 'success' denotes absence of forbidden reachability per the validators. Primary confirmatory test: exact McNemar-style paired test (alpha=0.05) with bootstrap percentile confidence intervals. Deviation disclosure: the preregistration planned 1,000 bootstrap resamples for CI estimation but the final analysis used 10,000 resamples to reduce Monte Carlo sampling error at negligible additional deterministic compute cost; this deviation is recorded in the analysis log (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; SHA-256: dd8abbbb86f85e67896baed7ac7c946ca260bffa3ff8d919a8ffb6cf31773be5) and is reported here.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the run completed all planned episodes (600 episodes = 300 pairs × 2 conditions), used model_calls_used = 300 (maximum_model_calls allowed = 600), and recorded zero failed episodes (see deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA-256: d5f2a8d1a1ebb7f4494b66533e3d4cb3bb21fbc85696a155787a3a82c4d25ea9). Primary outcome: complete_pair_count = 300; baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] computed from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Repair activity: under the preregistered GVR logic a repair would be attempted only if a validator reported forbidden reachability; across the run validators never reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate, so no repair prompts were generated and no repair calls were applied. Artifact evidence: per-episode validator_trace entries show repair_applied = false and repair_prompt_sha256 = null for representative episodes (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). Model-call accounting: the shared-initial generation contract produced a single LLM call per pair (provider_call audit records stage_counts 'shared_initial_generation' = 300), so median guarded-model-call overhead was zero.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the confirmatory null is degenerate because the baseline already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all preregistered tasks; with zero discordant pairs the paired test cannot evaluate whether GVR repairs would rescue violating outputs in more failure-prone settings. This outcome stems from design choices frozen in the preregistration: (a) the shared_initial_candidate contract (one shared LLM draw per pair) conserves model-call budget but reduces independent draws that might produce discordant erroneous outputs; the provider_call_audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json records 'shared_initial_generation' = 300. (b) The adversarial variants used here did not produce verifier-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators. Implications: experiments that aim to stress-test verifier-in-the-loop efficacy should adopt one or more of: stronger/algorithmic adversarial intent generators, independent-condition generation or larger repair budgets (to exercise repair paths), multiple LLM families, and stronger execution oracles. Reproducibility and provenance: all raw model outputs, validator traces, and analysis CSVs are archived; readers can inspect the full manifest at execution/execution_manifest.json and representative raw results at execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256: 36ea4a5dfa90384f2a388cba4f39bf193bb3c150ea22ca60957facb20ca960f1).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation using gpt-5-mini over 300 matched intents. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: both baseline and guarded conditions passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11=300). Critically, the verifier never reported violations and the repair path was never invoked under the chosen task set and execution contract. This result underscores that benchmark difficulty and experimental contract choices (shared vs independent generation, adversarial potency, repair budget, verifier strength) materially determine whether verifier-in-the-loop architectures can demonstrate benefits. We therefore recommend more adversarial, production-representative workloads and experimental contracts that ensure the repair path is exercised before drawing broader conclusions about verifier efficacy in NetOps security.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better stress the repair path.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.

Validator detail disclosure: per-episode artifacts record validator_id='deterministic_netops_validator_v5' and validator_version='5.0' and the primary decision rule used in this study is the forbidden-reachability predicate as evaluated by the validators (see execution/scoring/*.json). Precise Batfish container-image tags and the exact Batfish policy file names/configuration are preserved in the archived execution manifest and validator artifacts (execution/execution_manifest.json); the manuscript reports the defender-oriented decision rule and archival locations but does not list low-level container tags inline.

Contamination risk: deterministic duplicate and fuzzy-deduplication checks were applied prior to execution and analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports no flagged items; residual training-data overlap with hosted LLMs cannot be entirely excluded and is treated in archived sensitivity analyses.
